newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN rights envoys hope to see Nigeria's jailed Ogonis.
newsitem.headline: UN rights envoys hope to see Nigeria's jailed Ogonis.

text.p: Two U.N. human rights investigators who have been seeking access to Nigeria since the execution of dissident writer Ken Saro-Wiwa in 1995 have been invited by the government to visit this month, the world body said on Friday.
They will look into "serious allegations" of extrajudicial killings and hope to interview jailed opposition figures and 19 leaders of the Ogoni tribe, according to U.N. sources.

The 19 Ogoni, said to be detained in poor conditions at Port Harcourt and in deteriorating health, also face the death sentence, they added. They were followers of Saro-Wiwa and members of the Movement to Save the Ogoni People (MOSOP).

Nigeria drew worldwide outrage in November 1995 when it hanged Saro-Wiwa and eight Ogoni minority rights activists after their conviction in the 1994 murder of four pro-government tribal chiefs. Their trial was judged unfair by international judicial experts, but the defendants had no right to appeal.
They had been campaigning for compensation for Ogoniland in south-eastern Nigeria for oil produced there by mutli-national corporations. The 19 are also charged with the four murders.

"There is also concern that the tribunal before which these people are appearing lack independence and impartiality. There are questions of access to legal counsel and other due process questions," a U.N. source told Reuters.

Bacre Waly Ndiaye, U.N. special rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions and Param Cumaraswamy, U.N. special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, will travel to Nigeria February 23 to March 5.
They hope to see prominent pro-democracy oposition figures, including human rights defenders and lawyers, U.N. sources said.

It was not clear whether the investigators would have access to detained presidential claimant Moshood Abiola, who is charged with treason. He has been detained since June 1994 after a previous army government annuled a 1993 presidential poll.
But a U.N. statement which announced the visit, set the tone by making clear that the U.N. investigators expected full access to detainees and non-governmental organisations.
"The fact-finding mission will be carried out pursuant to the standard terms of reference for fact-finding missions by special rapporteurs of the U.N. Commission on Human Rights."

"These terms of reference include provisions for the freedom of movement in the whole country, freedom of inquiry including access to all detention centres and contact with the full range of persons considered necessary for fulfilment of the mandate."
U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut told a news briefing:
"The investigators will go to Lagos and Abuja but also to regions where there has been excessive use of force which has led to various allegations."
Ndiaye will be going to Kano and Kaduna in the north, while Cumaraswamy will head south to Port Harcourt in the same state as oil-rich Ogoniland, where he hopes to check on the 19 Ogoni.
Cumaraswamy, a Malaysian lawyer, is concerned they are to be tried by a tribunal similar to the one which tried Saro-Wiwa.

"Nobody has seen them except in some court appearances. They apparently looked to be in very poor condition and have physical health problems, including diabetes and heart problems," a U.N. source told Reuters. "They lack access to legal counsel."

The investigators will report back to the U.N. Human Rights Commission. Nigeria will be one of the countries in the dock when the main U.N. human rights forum opens its annual six-week meeting in Geneva on March 10, according to U.N. sources.
The 53-member body last April censured Nigeria for violating fundamental freedoms of its citizens and called on Lagos to allow the two U.N. investigators to make a joint visit.
The U.N. General Assembly, in a resolution adopted in December 1996, called on Nigeria to cooperate immediately with the special rapporteurs to pave the way for their mission.
